title: Lesson 31: Apex Architecture: Service Layer, Domain, and Selector Patterns
description: How to organize Apex so a requirement change touches one class: a service layer that orchestrates processes, a domain layer that owns object behavior, and a selector layer that owns every SOQL query.

questions.question: A business operation must be callable from a UI, a batch job, and an API, and the object's calculation rules should be shared by all three callers. Where does each piece belong?
options: The service layer exposes the operation and the object's domain class holds the calculation.
The trigger owns the operation, because it runs for every record change on the object.
The selector class owns the operation, because it already queries the object for the caller.
Each entry point implements the rule for itself, so the logic stays close to the caller that needs it.
questions.explanation: The service layer is the process entry point every caller shares, and object behavior belongs in the domain class so the trigger and the service cannot disagree.

questions.question: Why is a trigger a poor home for nontrivial business logic?
options: Because a trigger is invoked for a single record at a time, so it cannot handle a whole collection.
Because a trigger cannot be called from other entry points, so its logic gets copied and drifts.
Because the platform forbids queries inside a trigger body.
Because trigger logic cannot be tested or deployed with changesets.
questions.explanation: A trigger is not a reusable class, so logic placed there cannot be shared with other entry points and ends up duplicated and inconsistent across them.

questions.question: A bulk load inserts thousands of records and the object's logic queries once per record. What does the selector pattern change?
options: It moves the query into the trigger so it runs once per transaction.
It removes the need to bulkify because the selector caches each record it loads.
It centralizes the query behind set-based criteria for the whole collection.
It splits the large load into single-record transactions so each one stays under the limits.
questions.explanation: Triggers run in bulk, so a query per record spends the shared budget in proportion to load size; a selector that takes a collection and queries once keeps the logic bulk safe.
